justification: All three round-1 hard-rule findings are fixed and I independently re-verified each against the live source rather than trusting the diff. (1) File.Replace: I fetched https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.file.replace in full and the Remarks section reads verbatim 'If the sourceFileName and destinationFileName are on different volumes, this method raises an exception.' The article's quoted clause -- 'if the `sourceFileName` and `destinationFileName` are on different volumes, this method raises an exception' -- matches character-for-character (only the leading capitalization differs, which is normal for a quote spliced mid-sentence). The invented 'must be on the same drive' wording is gone. (2) ext4 journal: I fetched https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/ext4/journal.html and the live sentence reads 'Should the system crash during the second slow write, the journal can be replayed all the way to the latest commit record, guaranteeing the atomicity of whatever gets written through the journal to the disk.' The article now quotes 'second slow write' verbatim -- the bracketed '[real]' substitution is gone, replaced with the source's actual word. (3) File.Move: the article no longer claims the documentation 'draws the matching line for .NET' or states a same-volume move 'is a single filesystem operation' as if sourced. It now reads 'File.Move's own documentation describes only the expensive path for .NET: "moving the file across disk volumes is equivalent to copying the file and deleting it from the source if the copying was successful" ("File.Move Method"). It says nothing directly about the same-volume case, but the implication is that the copy-and-delete fallback is needed specifically because crossing volumes rules out the cheap path...' -- I fetched the live File.Move page and the quoted clause matches verbatim; the claim about the same-volume case is now explicitly marked as the article's own inference ('it says nothing directly', 'the implication is'), not presented as the documentation's words. This is honest and no longer a fabricated-attribution problem. The diff also shows two unrequested improvements: the block-group-descriptor sentence now carries an inline citation to a real quote instead of an uncited paraphrase, and the 'data=ordered' exercise's quote (previously floating without a citation marker) now has one. I independently fetched https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/ext4/blockgroup.html to check the new quote and found one residual, very minor fidelity slip: the source reads '...It is continuous range of blocks large enough to contain sb.s_inodes_per_group * sb.s_inode_size bytes' (the source's own grammar omits an article before 'continuous'), and the piece quotes it as 'a continuous range of blocks large enough to contain sb.s_inodes_per_group * sb.s_inode_size bytes' -- one inserted word ('a') that doesn't appear in the source's own sentence. It changes nothing about meaning and most plausibly is an unconscious grammar-smoothing rather than a deliberate alteration, but strictly it is still a quoted string inside quotation marks that isn't a character-exact copy of the source, so I am logging it rather than waving it through given this article's specific history on this exact failure mode. It is not comparable in kind to the two round-1 violations (one invented phrase never on the page at all, one word substituted for a different word that changes the sentence's sense) and does not by itself justify another hard cap. Everything else holds up on a fresh full read: no filler intro/outro (opens by handing off directly from the virtual-memory article's stated boundary), no restated title, no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways headings, no ad code, no keyword stuffing. Heading style compared against the other four operating-systems siblings (concurrency-race-conditions-locks.md, cpu-scheduling.md, processes-and-threads.md, virtual-memory.md): question-form headings echo virtual-memory.md's convention but on entirely disjoint content (disk-side structures, journaling, application durability vs. paging mechanics), while concurrency and processes-and-threads use declarative headings -- not a templated, mass-produced pattern across the pillar. The two exercises are individually named ('What "ordered" actually promises', 'The version that looks fine until it isn't'), vary in form (predict-then-explain vs. a conceptual which-claim-holds question), and neither shows its output panel above its solution. Cross-links: the write-ahead-logging link resolves to a real, published (draft: false) anchor in databases/transactions-and-acid.md that I confirmed exists verbatim ('## How does write-ahead logging change durability and concurrency?'); the virtual-memory link points at an article that is draft: true only in this stale worktree (already flipped to draft: false on the integration branch per this repo's own history) -- the writer's crosslinks file explicitly flags this exact staleness risk and tells the integrator how to handle it, which is the correct, disclosed way to handle a cross-branch race, not a defect. docs/crosslinks/operating-systems/file-systems.md is sensible and scoped, with an explicit 'boundaries with planned siblings' section preventing near-duplicate coverage with virtual-memory.md and the not-yet-written memory-hierarchy-and-caches article. run-code.mjs passes clean (blocks=8, executed=4), matching round 1's result.
